title: Batching and KV-cache Interaction: Latency Playbook
content:
Purpose:
Quick working playbook for isolating end-to-end latency regressions that appear to involve interactions between request batching and the KV-prefix cache. This is intentionally informal — notes, hypotheses, and quick experiment run recipes so on-call and perf engineers can reproduce and triage faster.

Background/context:
- We saw a p95 and p99 uplift in several customer-facing traces over the past 36 hours for mixed workload endpoints (chat + short completions).
- Symptoms: p50 unchanged, p95 up ~25-40ms, p99 up ~120-180ms on average. Spike correlates with a deployment that adjusted default batch-window from 6ms -> 8ms and enabled async prefetch for KV cache (opt-in).
- Hypothesis: under certain seq-len mixes and request interarrival distributions, increased batching window + asynchronous KV prefetch increases stage concurrency and causes head-of-line blocking or GC pressure in the KV cache layer, leading to tail latency amplification.

What to measure (quick checklist):
- Reproduce trace groups: collect 1k traces per configuration (baseline vs suspect).
- Capture per-stage timings at high resolution: parse & export stage timings for: ingress, routing, batching-wait, batch-assemble, kv-lookup (sync), kv-prefetch (async), model-invoke, kv-insert, response-serialize, egress.
- Track resource signals: GPU queue depth, CPU steal, per-process RSS/heap growth during experiment windows, number of active asyncio tasks.
- Correlate seq_len, token_count with latency buckets — create small pivot table: seqlen_bin x stage_p95.

Replay configuration to reproduce (fast):
- Use synthetic frontier: 60% short (seqlen=8-32), 30% medium (seqlen=64-256), 10% long (>512). Poisson arrival with mean lambda tuned to endpoint QPS from prod (use qps=60 for small cluster test).
- Run variants:
  A) baseline: batch-window=6ms, kv_prefetch=off
  B) suspect: batch-window=8ms, kv_prefetch=on (async)
  C) stress: batch-window=8ms, kv_prefetch=on, burst qps +30%
- Each run: 15 minutes warmup, 30 minutes measured. Export traces with unique correlation-id prefix.

Key artifacts to produce from runs:
- Per-stage p50/p95/p99 CSVs (rows: stage, cols: p50, p95, p99)
- Waterfall sample traces for the worst 10 p99 traces (include raw event list and timestamps)
- Residence-time histogram for batching-wait stage by sequence-length bin
- Async task backlog over time (samples/sec)

Representative (toy) per-stage CSV (paste this into quick analysis):
stage,p50_ms,p95_ms,p99_ms
ingress,0.5,1.0,1.6
routing,0.7,1.2,2.4
batching-wait,3.1,12.4,45.8
batch-assemble,0.9,1.3,2.0
kv-lookup-sync,2.2,3.5,6.5
kv-prefetch-async,0.0,0.0,120.7
model-invoke,15.2,15.9,18.3
kv-insert,0.6,1.1,2.2
response-serialize,0.4,0.8,1.5
egress,0.3,0.4,0.9

Notes on that CSV: kv-prefetch-async shows bulk of tail in this hypothetical run (p99 120ms). In practice prefetch async shouldn't be on the critical path; if it is, something is awaiting its completion downstream or a lock/queue is saturated.

Possible root causes (ranked):
1) Head-of-line blocking due to limited batch assembly worker threads: a long async prefetch task holds a per-batch lock or consumes a worker slot needed to finalize small batches.
2) Prefetch backpressure: async prefetch tasks enqueue a completion callback on the same event loop that handles batching finalization; under high concurrency the callback queue grows and processing stalls.
3) Memory/GC pressure: increased concurrency increases transient allocations (buffers, futures), causing occasional stop-the-world GC on Python runtime or alloc contention in native KV library.
4) Kernel-level scheduling: change in interarrival to allow bursts aligning poorly with our user-space batching timer causing synchronized wakeups and contention.
5) External KV latency tail amplification (third-party store) combined with our prefetch policy causing more in-flight requests than before.

Quick experiments to differentiate causes (ordered cheap->expensive):
- Disable async prefetch entirely (A vs B). If tail disappears => prefetch implicated.
- Toggle prefetch worker pool size to a very small and very large value. If larger pool reduces tail => worker-exhaustion hypothesis.
- Add per-batch timeouts around prefetch and log if callbacks delayed beyond threshold (e.g., 50ms).
- Instrument event-loop queue length: use tracemalloc and asyncio.get_running_loop().call_soon queue length metrics. Correlate with latency spikes.
- Run with Python GC debug logs (PYTHONMALLOC=debug or gc.set_debug) and inspect GC pause timestamps aligning with tail traces.
- Shadow traces with direct KV store sampling (p99 of KV store) — if KV store p99 independent and high, this points external store.

Example trace excerpt (raw, simplified):
[trace-id=20251118-hex-0001]
0.0000 ingress start
0.0005 routing start
0.0012 routing end
0.0012 batching enqueue
0.0049 batching-wait start
0.0143 batching-wait end (batch formed w/ 12 reqs)
0.0143 batch-assemble start
0.0150 batch assembled
0.0150 kv-prefetch async kicked (fire-and-forget: task_id t-981)
0.0151 model-invoke start
0.0306 model-invoke end
0.0307 kv-insert start
0.0313 kv-insert end
0.0314 response-serialize
0.0318 egress
async callback t-981 completed at 0.1567  <-- large completion latency observed

Interpretation: model path not blocked but async completion took 125ms later. Why did async callback tail matter? Two possibilities: callback ran on same loop that also serializes responses or cleanup steps are performed synchronously later (bug). Need to grep code paths that call await on prefetch futures or that rely on shared lock released by callback.

Instrumentation TODOs (code pointers):
- Add high frequency logpoints in batch finalize path: record number of outstanding async prefetch tasks and their ages. File: runtime/batcher/batcher.py:finalize_batch()
- Add metrics: batch_prefetch_inflight_count, batch_prefetch_age_p95/p99. Export via statsd.
- Add trace span around prefetch enqueue and actual callback execution, include thread-id and loop-id.

Mitigations (temporary & long-term):
- Immediate rollback option: revert batch-window to 6ms + disable prefetch for affected fleet. Communicate rollback decision to SRE and customer success.
- Short-term patch: ensure async prefetch callbacks are scheduled on dedicated worker threadpool (off the main event loop) and make prefetch truly fire-and-forget with no synchronous join.
- Long-term: redesign prefetch to expose backpressure signals and bounded concurrency; add admission control so prefetch cannot create unbounded in-flight requests.

Acceptance criteria for mitigation (what success looks like):
- After mitigation, p95 returns within 5ms of baseline and p99 within 20ms of baseline for the same synthetic workload.
- No increase in error rates or timeouts.
- No excessive increase in overall token cost.

Open questions / notes to self:
- Are there specific customers who started using prefetch opt-in flags in last 48h? (CS to check)
- Confirm whether any model servers were upgraded at same time (possible interacting change).
- Check infra-level scheduling change in kube autoscaler configs rolled out last week.

Next steps (owner map):
- Anika: run the replay plan B vs A, collect artifacts and upload to CONFLUENCE-7554 (today).
- Marco: add the high-frequency logpoints and metric hooks; prepare quick patch to schedule callbacks off main loop (tomorrow).
- Leah: talk to CS for customer opt-ins and to SRE about rolling back batch-window config if needed (today).

Appendix: quick grep checklist (use these searches locally)
- grep -R "prefetch" runtime | grep -E "async|await|callback|thread"
- inspect batcher finalizer for locks: grep -n "finalize" runtime/batcher | xargs sed -n '1,240p'

Rough notes / heuristics (brainstorm):
- When batch-window grows slightly, more requests join the same batch which increases variance in batch finalization latency (one long request can hold whole batch). For small-seqlen heavy traffic, this effect is more noticeable because model-invoke latency is small relative to prefetch noise.
- Async conveniences can hide tail work; always verify that "fire-and-forget" work has no side-channel that can impact request completion path (locks, shared buffers, allocs).

End of playbook (working doc).

-- Anika
